Since the end of World War II, the American mining companies (and others, too) have spent a great deal of time, effort and money here and abroad in the exploration for, and development of, new material resources. Now, for the first time in the last thirty years, the world has finally caught up with itself in that the supply of basic earth materials is sufficient to meet the immediate demand. This situation, however, will not long continue. If the U.S. is to maintain a competitive position (in any field) among the community of nations, it must have access to an assured supply of raw materials at reasonable prices. I urge you, therefore, to work out some licensing arrangement that would permit the exploration geologist to conduct his studies without undue restriction.
I do not know what ethical or moral problems there may be in denying use to some while allowing others freedom from such restrictions. I do contend, however, that there is a real difference between simple "joy-riding" and travel for the purpose of making a living. I also maintain that the exploration geologist does perform useful and necessary work, not only for himself and his company, but for the country.
Sincerely yours,
Stewart R. Wallace
